title: The Model Millionaire
tagline: A penniless gentleman gives away his last coin to a beggar-model — and Wilde’s comedy turns on what the beggar is.

overview.intro: Oscar Wilde’s “The Model Millionaire” is a comedy of appearances in which generosity is the only investment that pays. Hughie Erskine is charming, well-mannered and permanently unsuccessful: every profession he tries fails, and the father of the woman he loves demands a fortune before the wedding. Calling on his artist friend Trevor, Hughie finds him painting a beggar from the streets, and moved by the old man’s destitution he gives him the cab fare he was carrying — his last coin. The sitter turns out to be Count Baron von Hausberg, one of the richest men in Europe, in disguise; within a day Hughie receives a wedding gift of the exact sum he needs. The chapter follows the plot, the characters and Wilde’s central joke: in a world that judges by surfaces, the man who looked poorest was richest, and the only man who behaved generously was the one with nothing.

learn.title: Before you read: Wilde’s comedy of appearances

blocks.text: Wilde’s fiction delights in reversals: the moment when the surface of things is lifted and the reader discovers that everything has been read backwards. “The Model Millionaire” is built on two of his favourite subjects — the tyranny of money in marriage, and the way society mistakes appearance for fact. Read the opening portrait of Hughie Erskine as Wildean catalogue: every charm listed carefully, every failure listed with equal care, and the gap between the two treated as society’s error rather than the young man’s. Then watch the studio scene, where Wilde stages his reversal through an act of pure sympathy. The comedy works because Hughie never suspects anything: he gives the coin because a man is cold and old, not because a plan is in view, and that innocence of motive is precisely what the story rewards. The title tells you the joke in advance — a millionaire posing as a model — and the pleasure lies in waiting for the disguise to lift and for the world to re-sort itself accordingly.

items: Wilde reverses surfaces and realities: poor looks rich, rich looks poor.
Hughie’s catalogue of charms and failures satirises a money-judging society.
The studio scene is the hinge: generosity performed without a thought of return.
The title announces the disguise; the structure delivers the reversal.

learn.title: The story in outline: the poverty, the studio, the gift, the gift returned

blocks.text: Published summaries give the story in four movements. First, the situation of Hughie Erskine: he is handsome and agreeable but has failed at everything he has attempted — the army, law, the stock exchange, even literature — and lives on small means. He loves Laura Merton, and her father, a retired colonel with a temper and a condition, will consent to the marriage only if Hughie possesses ten thousand pounds; the sum is impossible for him, and the demand makes the wedding a joke between the young couple. Second, the visit: Hughie calls on his friend Trevor, an artist who is painting an old model — a beggar taken from the streets — for a picture of beggars. Third, the gesture: the sight of the poor old sitter moves Hughie, who, on his way out, presses his last coin into the man’s hand; it is the whole of his cab fare and, in effect, his last possession. Fourth, the reversal: the beggar is Count Baron von Hausberg, enormously wealthy and amused by the world’s manners; the next day a messenger arrives with a gift of ten thousand pounds and a brief note approving Hughie’s character. The wedding, the summaries agree, follows shortly.

learn.title: The characters: Hughie, the count, Trevor and Laura

blocks.text: Hughie Erskine is Wilde’s ideal of unworldly charm: he fails at every profession not from stupidity but because application bores him, and he remains cheerful, courteous and incapable of calculation. His gift in the studio is characteristic — he never weighs the cost, because another person’s need arrives before his own. Count Baron von Hausberg is the story’s engine of reversal: a millionaire so tired of being flattered for his money that he disguises himself as a beggar to discover how people behave when money seems absent, and he rewards Hughie because Hughie alone behaved as though the old man were simply a man. Published summaries note that the count’s pleasure is aesthetic — he buys the scene he has witnessed, not the man. Trevor, the painter, is the practical friend: he takes the beggar from the streets for his picture, introduces the two worlds, and asks for nothing. Laura Merton is devotion with a father attached — she loves Hughie, jokes about the impossible condition, and waits. And the colonel, Laura’s father, embodies the money-principle the story is interrogating: his consent is priced in exact figures.

items.text: Hughie gives away his cab fare to a stranger because the stranger is old and cold.
items.note: Generosity with no calculation — the quality the count buys.

items.text: The count sits in disguise to see how he would be treated without his money.
items.note: The reversal is engineered by the rich man, not by fortune alone.

learn.title: Irony: who is the model, and who is the millionaire?

blocks.text: The story’s ironies are layered, and an examination answer should separate them. Situational irony: the beggar turns out to be a millionaire, and the penniless gentleman turns out to have an income waiting for him — appearance and fact exchange places completely. Verbal irony sits in Wilde’s titles and captions: “the model millionnaire” applies to the old man posing as a pauper, while Hughie, who models nothing, is treated by the world as worthless. Dramatic irony comes from the reader’s position in the studio: we are told who the sitter is or can guess it, while Hughie gives his coin in ignorance, so the same gesture reads as foolishness and as wisdom at once. And a quieter irony governs the ending: the count’s gift is presented as approval of Hughie’s character, yet it is also a purchase — money confirming an act done without money — which leaves the reader wondering whether even generosity can stay unpolluted in a world where everything has a price. Wilde never resolves that last question, and the ambiguity is deliberate: the comedy is warm, but the arithmetic underneath it is cold.

items: Situational: beggar is a millionaire; the rich man is the beggar.
Verbal: the title applies to the disguised count.
Dramatic: the reader can guess the truth Hughie cannot.
Final ambiguity: is the gift approval, or is it a purchase?

learn.title: Themes: appearances, generosity and true nobility

blocks.text: Appearances against reality is the governing theme: Trevor’s painting is literally a picture of surfaces, and the story keeps asking who people are when their surfaces are wrong — the beggar who is a count, the gentleman who is a pauper, the colonel who is a price-list. Generosity is the theme the plot rewards: Hughie’s coin is the only uncalculated act in a story full of calculations, and the narrative answers it with the exact sum he needs, a symmetry Wilde intends to be both fairy-tale and satirical. True nobility follows from the two: the count, though the richest man in the room, is only impressed by behaviour that has never heard of his money, and the story quietly defines worth as conduct rather than balance. A careful answer will also note the pressure the themes come under — the reward does arrive as money, after all, so the story celebrates purity while paying for it in the coin of the world it criticises. That double edge is Wilde’s signature and the surest sign the theme has been understood.

learn.title: For the examination, and what to verify yourself

blocks.text: Plot questions are common in this story and they punish loose ordering: Hughie’s condition, the demand of ten thousand pounds, the studio visit, the coin, the count’s message, the wedding — keep that chain exact and name the sum every time. Character questions usually pair Hughie with the count, and the strongest answers contrast their motives: one acts without thinking, the other thinks of everything. Technique questions about irony are where the marks multiply — name the type of irony, locate it in a scene, and state its effect on the reader. Title questions deserve preparation too: explain both meanings of “model” (the sitter in a studio, and the standard of behaviour Hughie sets) and both meanings of “millionnaire” (the man who is one, and the man who is about to be made one). Finally, this page follows published summaries rather than the text itself: verify every detail you plan to reproduce against your prescribed edition, since accuracy about the story’s facts is what short answers reward.

questions.prompt: How much must Hughie possess before Colonel Merton will consent to the marriage?
questions.explanation: The colonel’s condition is exact: Hughie must be worth ten thousand pounds before the wedding can be consented to — the figure the story ends by supplying.
questions.commonMistake: Do not answer an income; the demand is a capital sum.

questions.prompt: What is the old man in Trevor’s studio when Hughie first sees him?
options: A beggar from the streets posing as a model
A dressed count visiting the artist
questions.answer: A beggar from the streets posing as a model
questions.explanation: Trevor has taken an old beggar from the streets to paint him in a study of beggars; the man’s real identity as Count von Hausberg is withheld from Hughie.
questions.commonMistake: The count is disguised; nobody in the studio but the count knows the truth.

questions.prompt: What does Hughie give to the old model?
options: His last coin, the whole of his cab fare
A bank note from his savings
questions.answer: His last coin, the whole of his cab fare
questions.explanation: Hughie presses his remaining coin — the fare for his cab — into the old man’s hand, giving away the whole of what he carries.
questions.commonMistake: The gift’s significance lies in it being everything he had, not in its amount.

questions.prompt: Why does the count disguise himself as a beggar?
options: To see how people treat him when he appears to have no money
Because Trevor asked him to pose
questions.answer: To see how people treat him when he appears to have no money
questions.explanation: Published summaries describe the count as weary of being valued for his purse, so he sits in disguise to watch behaviour unhindered by money — and he rewards the one man who passed the test.
questions.commonMistake: Trevor does not know the identity either; the disguise is the count’s own device.

questions.prompt: The millionaire who poses as a beggar-model is Count Baron von ______.
questions.explanation: The sitter is Count Baron von Hausberg, described as one of the richest men in Europe, amusing himself with a disguise.
questions.commonMistake: Spell the name carefully — it is the story’s reversal in one word.

questions.prompt: Why is Hughie Erskine called “the model millionnaire” in the story’s scheme?
questions.answer: Because the phrase applies twice. The literal model in the studio is the disguised count, who is the actual millionaire; and Hughie, though penniless, is the model of the behaviour the story admires — generous, uncalculated and noble in conduct — so he is a millionaire of character long before the gift arrives.
questions.explanation: Both meanings must be shown: the studio sitter and the example Hughie sets, which is what the title question tests.
questions.commonMistake: Answering only “because the count was the model” misses the second, moral meaning.

questions.prompt: How does Hughie react to the colonel’s demand?
questions.answer: He takes it cheerfully rather than bitterly: he and Laura treat the impossible sum as a joke between them, since neither has any money and the condition is plainly beyond him. He continues to visit Laura and to hope, while making no plan to acquire the ten thousand pounds, because calculation of that kind is foreign to his nature.
questions.explanation: The reaction — amusement instead of despair — is what characterises Hughie, and it must be linked to his unworldly nature.
questions.commonMistake: Do not write that he resolves to earn it; his lack of a plan is the point.

questions.prompt: Describe the scene in Trevor’s studio and Hughie’s part in it.
questions.answer: Hughie calls on his friend Trevor, a painter, and finds him at work on a picture of beggars, for which an old man taken from the streets is sitting as a model. The studio conversation shows Trevor at his practical best — he paints the poor without sentimentality and asks nothing of his friend — while the old sitter, wrapped and worn, is presented to Hughie as simply a man enduring the discomfort of posing. The sight moves Hughie, who is by temperament untouched by calculation: on his way out he presses his last coin into the old man’s hands, telling himself that the cab can walk. Published summaries stress that he gives without any suspicion of a reward — the cab fare is his entire wealth that day, and the gesture leaves him stranded rather than enriched. The scene is the story’s hinge because it performs the test the count has designed: with money removed from the picture, behaviour shows its actual character, and Hughie’s conduct is the only part of it that passes.
questions.explanation: The description covers setting, characters, gesture and cost, then explains the scene’s function as the count’s test, which is the analytical depth the question allows.
questions.commonMistake: Do not omit what the gift costs Hughie — the fare is what gives the act its meaning.

questions.prompt: How does the count reward Hughie, and what does the reward suggest about the story’s view of money?
questions.answer: The next day a messenger arrives at Hughie’s rooms carrying ten thousand pounds — the exact sum the colonel demanded — with a brief note that approves Hughie’s conduct and intends the money as a wedding gift. The reward solves the plot with fairy-tale precision: the amount is not generous but exact, which is Wilde’s joke about a world that runs on figures. What the reward suggests about money is deliberately double-edged. On one side, the story celebrates a transaction in which moral worth is finally converted into its worldly equivalent: the uncalculated coin buys the calculated sum, and the man who never schemed receives what scheming could not have earned. On the other side, the conversion is itself troubling — even Hughie’s purity is ultimately priced, paid for and settled in cash, so the society the story mocks has managed to put a figure on virtue as well. Published study guides read the ending as warm; a strong answer adds that its warmth comes with the author’s characteristic smile about who, in the end, is doing the buying.
questions.explanation: The answer gives the reward precisely and then reads it in both directions — celebration and irony — which is what the question’s last clause asks for.
questions.commonMistake: Do not stop at “generosity is rewarded”; the double edge is the higher-mark observation.

questions.prompt: Every character in the story judges or is judged by money. Discuss, with reference to the events.
questions.answer: The story is organised as a sequence of money-judgments, each of which the plot then corrects. Colonel Merton judges Hughie by the only standard he recognises — ten thousand pounds — and prices his daughter’s consent accordingly, reducing marriage to arithmetic. Society judges Hughie by his failures, listing the professions he has not kept, so that charm without income counts as worthlessness. Hughie alone judges by no money-standard at all: he reads the old man as cold and old, gives his cab fare, and never once calculates — and it is precisely this blindness to value that the count is seeking when he sits in disguise, tired of being liked for his balance. Trevor judges nothing; he works. And the count, the richest judge of all, rigs the experiment so that money is removed from the picture, then rewards the single man who behaved as though money had never existed. The ending answers each judgment with its opposite: the priced marriage is funded, the worthless man is given a fortune, and the beggar proves to be the purchaser of the scene he witnessed. What remains ambiguous is the final judgment itself — the count’s gift restores the money-principle at the very moment it seems to defeat it, because virtue, too, is paid in cash. Wilde’s society, the story implies, cannot even reward innocence without sending a bill.
questions.explanation: The answer tracks every character’s money-judgment and its correction by the plot, then confronts the final ambiguity — a complete analytical treatment rather than a theme summary.
questions.commonMistake: Do not present the ending as simple justice; the story’s last irony is that justice is invoiced.
